t: During the period beginning on the date of the enactment of this Act and ending on February 28, 1981, the public debt limit set forth in the first sentence of section 21 of the Second Liberty Bond Act (31 U.S.C. 757b) shall be temporarily increased by $525,000,000,000.

fable.w: This section only temporarily raises the statutory public debt limit by a fixed amount for a set period. No outside party (states, the public, experts, companies) is consulted or given a role, and there is no rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue. There is no real tempting reading here; the text is purely a fiscal adjustment made directly by Congress.
fable.s: the public debt limit set forth in the first sentence of section 21 of the Second Liberty Bond Act (31 U.S.C. 757b) shall be temporarily increased by $525,000,000,000.

opus.w: This section only raises the public debt limit by a set amount for a limited time. It does not call for consultation, hearings, comment periods, rulemaking, advisory bodies or any right to sue, so no one outside the federal government takes part in a decision. Any assumption that fiscal changes involve stakeholder input has no support in the text.
opus.s: the public debt limit set forth in the first sentence of section 21 of the Second Liberty Bond Act (31 U.S.C. 757b) shall be temporarily increased by $525,000,000,000.

qwen_chat.w: This section simply mandates a temporary increase in the statutory public debt limit. It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation with entities outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or experts) before or during this action. The decision is made entirely by Congress through the enactment of the statute.
qwen_chat.s: During the period beginning on the date of the enactment of this Act and ending on February 28, 1981, the public debt limit set forth in the first sentence of section 21 of the Second Liberty Bond Act (31 U.S.C. 757b) shall be temporarily increased by $525,000,000,000.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing the public debt limit is a major federal decision that should involve public input. However, the text itself contains no mechanism for such input; it is a unilateral legislative adjustment.
